judgeRationales.scenarioName: Catches compound allocations in recursive number converter with ToLower
judgeRationales.rationale: B performs a substantive, largely targeted hot-path performance review with actionable fixes and positive findings. Its site-count wording has a minor internal inconsistency, but it is overwhelmingly more useful and correct than A, which failed to access the available code and returned no analysis.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Detects Aggregate+Replace chain and struct missing IEquatable
judgeRationales.rationale: A is concise, covers all core bottlenecks, and its recommendations are generally safer. B adds useful detail, but several claims/recommendations reduce reliability: its replacement code changes matching semantics with OrdinalIgnoreCase, its exponent table incorrectly maps P to 14 rather than 15, and the suggested explicit 'static sealed' declaration is invalid/redundant for a static class. Those correctness issues outweigh B's added scan detail.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Detects CurrentCulture comparer and compiled regex budget in inflection rules
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: A, reverse: tie). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Detects compiled regex startup budget and regex chain allocations
judgeRationales.rationale: B is more complete, prioritized, and directly addresses the major compiled-regex-budget issue more clearly, while covering all requested hot-path findings. A has a more credible Pascalize implementation and is more concise, but it underemphasizes the overall compiled-regex budget and leaves the dominant Underscore chain largely intact. B's proposed one-pass code and minor JVM wording should be reviewed for correctness, so the advantage is modest.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Finds StringComparison.Ordinal missing and FrozenDictionary opportunities
judgeRationales.rationale: B is more complete on the relevant hot-path concatenations and provides more concrete source locations and fixes. Its added thread-safety issue is conditional on shared concurrent use and its severity is overstated, while sealing recommendations are more speculative, so the advantage is modest rather than large.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Finds branched Replace chain in format string manipulation
judgeRationales.rationale: A actually inspected the source and supplied a prioritized, mostly concrete performance review, including the central repeated-Replace allocation issue and a remediation. B failed to access the available task source and returned only a request to paste it.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Finds hot-path allocations in string humanization
judgeRationales.rationale: B covers all requested performance findings, particularly the omitted per-match ToLower and outer Dehumanize LINQ allocation, and supplies more concrete fixes. Some of B's ancillary claims are overstated (for example, the correctness framing around double humanization and the empty-string boxing note), so the gap is not overwhelming.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Finds per-call Dictionary allocation not hoisted to static
judgeRationales.rationale: B is more methodical, evidence-backed, and actionable, especially its viable static suffix-array redesign and allocation accounting. A covers the principal issues but includes a non-compilable/static-lambda sketch as written and adds less well-justified caching as a notable recommendation. B's extra unsealed-class item is speculative/minor, but does not undermine its stronger core review.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Finds repeated enumeration in time and collection formatting
judgeRationales.rationale: Both satisfy every requested finding well. B is slightly more complete and actionable, adding the Aggregate hot-path observation, both Take-based Join sites, source locations, and sensible benchmarking caveat. Some of its allocation wording and its List-based string.Join example are imprecise, so the advantage is modest rather than large.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Flags Span inconsistencies and compound method chains in truncation library
judgeRationales.rationale: A successfully locates and reviews the library, providing several concrete hot-path allocation and iteration findings with actionable rewrites. B incorrectly concludes no source is available and delivers no review.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: .NET Framework on Windows without admin privileges
judgeRationales.rationale: B aligns with the required limitations and gives the correct escalation path. A contains multiple material privilege/capability errors, especially its claimed no-admin PerfView CPU tracing and its assertion that dumps cannot be captured.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Assembly loading failure on Linux (.NET 8)
judgeRationales.rationale: B addresses the requested startup assembly-load trace with the correct high-level dotnet-trace launch strategy and assemblyloader event selection. A includes useful LoaderExceptions advice, but its tracing guidance uses an incorrect/questionable provider mask and introduces unsupported or misleading environment-variable claims. B's example should ideally launch `dotnet /path/to/your/app.dll` rather than the DLL alone, but it remains substantially closer to the required diagnostic procedure.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Container installation without .NET SDK
judgeRationales.rationale: A directly answers the central need with the documented aka.ms self-contained download, a runnable command, and viable collection steps. judgeRationales.scenarioName: Excessive GC on Linux (.NET 8)
judgeRationales.rationale: B directly supplies the correct gc-verbose collection workflow for .NET 8 Linux and explains how to inspect the resulting trace. A has useful ancillary advice, but misses the required profile and muddies trace-vs-dump guidance.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: HTTP 500s from downstream service on Linux (.NET 8)
judgeRationales.rationale: B directly and concretely answers the trace-collection question for a .NET 8 Linux process, explaining the relevant HTTP events, timing, and analysis workflow. judgeRationales.scenarioName: Hang or deadlock diagnosis on Linux

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Catches compound allocations in recursive number converter with ToLower
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses correctly identify the core issues: redundant .ToLower() calls, compound allocation from concatenation/interpolation, and the long.MinValue overflow bonus finding. Both recommend the same fixes. B is more thorough and precise, providing exact line numbers, a count of the 8 .ToLower() sites, and explicit enumeration of concatenation/interpolation sites, which better satisfies the counting and site-flagging criteria. A is well-reasoned and correct but less granular. The gap is modest, so B is slightly better overall.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Detects Aggregate+Replace chain and struct missing IEquatable
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses correctly identify the core hot-path bottlenecks (Math.Log10/Pow, linear exponent scan, replacement loop, formatting allocations). B is more thorough and precise: it names Aggregate, catches char.ToString() per-iteration allocation, provides structured severity/positive findings including a clean FrozenDictionary positive, and adds an appropriate disclaimer. A is solid and concise but misses char.ToString(), and its IEquatable/boxing remark is arguably incorrect. Neither nails IEquatable-boxing or the Contains short-circuit suggestion. Overall B is slightly better due to greater coverage of the rubric-specific items.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Detects CurrentCulture comparer and compiled regex budget in inflection rules
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: B, reverse: A). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Detects compiled regex startup budget and regex chain allocations
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses correctly identify the core hot-path issues (regex replace chains, per-match allocations, ToLower culture concerns) with solid remediation advice. However, B covers more rubric criteria comprehensively: it explicitly recognizes GeneratedRegex as a positive pattern and catches the InflectionRule per-instance regex compilation, both of which A misses entirely. B also traces additional call chains (Kebaberize, Camelize→Pascalize). A is cleaner and more focused, and its scan checklist in B contained some noisy/erroneous counts from failed rg commands, but B's substantive findings ultimately cover more of the rubric. B is slightly better overall."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Finds StringComparison.Ordinal missing and FrozenDictionary opportunities
judgeRationales.rationale: The task was to *review* the converters for performance, and B delivered a thorough, well-organized review with severity levels, file/line references, a scan checklist, and correct handling of all five rubric criteria. Critically, B also caught the long.MinValue infinite-recursion bug, a genuine high-severity defect. A instead performed edits without being asked, and its editing approach was haphazard — using perl/sed one-liners to patch source, introducing and then fixing corruption (turn 12-16), and never actually compiling (no csproj existed, so verification was skipped). A's changes risk leaving broken code, and it provided no verification that the file still compiles. B satisfies all rubric criteria clearly and adds valuable correctness findings while being methodical and honest with a disclaimer. B is much better for a review task. [Magnitude reduced to "slightly-better": the position-swapped pass judged this "slightly-better", so the more confident "much-better" was downgraded.]

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Finds branched Replace chain in format string manipulation
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses give solid, similar performance analyses covering the oversized struct and allocation-heavy formatting. B edges ahead by explicitly capturing the IEquatable positive finding (a rubric item A misses entirely) and being more precise about the Replace allocation count. Neither hits the #.## Replace flag or StringBuilder/string.Create suggestion. The gap is modest but B satisfies one more rubric criterion clearly.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Finds hot-path allocations in string humanization
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses cover the core allocation hot paths (LINQ pipeline, All scans, ToLower, Dehumanize concat, params array) at comparable quality and neither modified the fixture. The decisive differentiator is rubric criterion 6: B explicitly recognizes the span-based Concat helpers as an allocation-conscious positive finding, which A omits entirely. B also provides evidence-backed line references and a structured severity table. A's report is more prose-driven with additional valuable context (fast-path bug, caching strategy) but misses the positive-findings requirement. Overall B is slightly better on rubric coverage; A has some extra practical depth, so the gap is modest."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Finds per-call Dictionary allocation not hoisted to static
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses correctly identify the core issues (per-call dictionaries/closures in Farsi and Kurdish, Math.Pow constants, unsized lists, long.MinValue overflow). B additionally catches the string.Format boxing in FormatWithUnit (rubric #5), which A misses, and provides more precise, better-organized findings with line-level detail. B fully covers all 5 rubric criteria while A covers 4. B is slightly better overall.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Finds repeated enumeration in time and collection formatting
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are strong, methodical, and cover nearly all rubric criteria with accurate line references and no fixture modification. The key differentiator is that B explicitly identifies the Enumerable.Reverse static initialization anti-pattern (rubric criterion 4) with a concrete array-literal fix, correctly classifying it as one-time cost, while A omits it from its recommendations. B also adds a useful severity summary and a scan checklist. A slightly overstates the params count issue but its content is otherwise equivalent. Given B covers one additional rubric item that A misses, B is slightly better overall.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Flags Span inconsistencies and compound method chains in truncation library
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses cover the three core rubric items well and are of similar technical quality. A goes further with additional correct findings (non-positive length validation, marker-length >= edge case) that are genuine correctness/performance concerns, and it more clearly notes the inconsistent span usage across truncators. B is well-structured with a scan checklist and severity table, and includes a devirtualization observation, but adds boilerplate and doesn't clearly highlight the span inconsistency. A is slightly better overall due to more substantive coverage.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Identifies unsealed leaf classes and locale hierarchy patterns
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: B, reverse: A). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Handle .NET frames with no BuildId metadata
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses correctly handled the core task: identifying the .NET runtime frames, recognizing the absence of BuildId, explaining the symbol server limitation, suggesting alternatives, and avoiding fabrication. B is slightly better because it captured all 5 .NET frames (including libSystem.Native.so which A missed), verified its findings by actually running the symbolication script, and gave more complete/actionable guidance (readelf command, symbol server URL format). The methodology was also more thorough, using the skill and its parse tooling.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Recognize NativeAOT tombstone with app binary and libSystem.Native.so
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses satisfy all four rubric criteria well. A provides a cleaner, more complete answer including the concrete MS symbol server URL for libSystem.Native.so, which aligns with the rubric's expectation that this component is symbolizable via MS symbols. B did empirical verification (ran the skill script, hit a 404) which is more rigorous and honest, but framed the whole result as 'blocked,' which is slightly less helpful. The two are close, with A slightly better on rubric alignment and clarity while B is more thorough operationally."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Recognize tombstone with no .NET frames
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: B, reverse: A). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Reject iOS crash log as wrong format
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses correctly recognized the iOS crash log, declined the Android workflow, and avoided the symbol server. They are essentially equal on three of four criteria. Response A is slightly better because it provides a concrete, actionable atos command example, whereas Response B, while accurately citing the specific unresolved frame offsets, only describes the process without a usable command. The gap is minor.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Symbolicate .NET frames in an Android tombstone
judgeRationales.rationale: The core task was to symbolicate the frames and show function names and source locations. B successfully used the skill and its script to download symbols and produced a complete symbolicated backtrace (FailFast, do_icall, etc. with source lines) — fully accomplishing the task. A gave up, claiming the symbol download returned 404, and produced only instructions and unresolved offsets. While A's output was clearer about showing the URL and explicit llvm-symbolizer command, it failed the actual deliverable. B's successful symbolication is the decisive factor. Note B's successful download suggests A's 404 was likely due to using the wrong URL path (sym vs _.debug/elf-buildid-sym), which B's script handled correctly. [Magnitude reduced to "slightly-better": the position-swapped pass judged this "slightly-better", so the more confident "much-better" was downgraded.]

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Symbolicate CoreCLR frames in an Android tombstone
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses correctly identified CoreCLR, extracted the BuildId, and reported that frames couldn't be fully resolved. However, A provided the explicit symbol-server URL and the concrete llvm-symbolizer command with --obj and PC offsets, directly satisfying two rubric criteria that B did not present in its final answer. B actually attempted the download and correctly reported the 404, which is honest and grounded, but its final output lacks the explicit URL and llvm-symbolizer command the rubric rewards. A gives more actionable, rubric-aligned content, making it slightly better overall.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Symbolicate multi-thread tombstone
judgeRationales.rationale: The task was to symbolicate the .NET runtime frames. Response B actually completed the symbolication, producing real function names and source line locations for all 7 frames across all threads by downloading the correct symbols and running the automation script. Response A only identified the frames and BuildId, hit a 404 on the symbol server, and delivered raw PC offsets plus a command the user would have to run themselves — never producing the actual symbolicated output. B fulfilled the task; A left it incomplete.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Symbolicate tombstone with multiple .NET libraries and different BuildIds
judgeRationales.rationale: B actually performed the symbolication: it ran the skill's automation script, downloaded and verified the mono debug symbols, resolved 5 frames to real function names and source locations, and honestly noted the two libSystem BuildIds returned 404. Response A only produced instructions and hypothetical commands without executing anything, leaving the task unfinished. B delivers a genuinely symbolicated backtrace, which is the actual deliverable requested." [Magnitude reduced to "slightly-better": the position-swapped pass judged this "slightly-better", so the more confident "much-better" was downgraded.]

verdictEvidence.reason: Net win +33.3% (2W/0T/1L over 3 stimulus vote(s), sign test p=0.500), mean preference +13.3% across 3 paired run(s) — underpowered (3 counted stimulus vote(s); a credible verdict needs at least 5) — add distinct, discriminating stimuli; repeated runs do not increase task breadth

Parse .NET frames and locate dSYMs from an iOS crash log

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Investigate root cause of a .NET MAUI iOS crash
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses correctly diagnosed a SIGABRT/EXC_CRASH from an uncaught managed exception during MAUI startup, and both correctly noted the log lacks the managed exception type/message. B is slightly better because it explicitly identified the CoreCLR runtime by UUID and even fetched the matching CoreCLR dSYM from Microsoft's symbol server, directly addressing the CoreCLR-identification and symbolication rubric points. Neither gave explicit SDK-pack/NuGet dSYM paths, so the gap is modest.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Parse .NET frames and locate dSYMs from an iOS crash log
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses correctly parsed the crash log and produced valid, matching atos commands for libcoreclr. B's key advantage is that it actually located the debug symbols — downloading the UUID-matched dSYM from Microsoft's symbol server and verifying it was a valid arm64 Mach-O dSYM — directly fulfilling the 'locate the dSYM debug symbols' part of the task, whereas A concluded no symbols were available and gave only generic guidance. B also handled the two-part JSON format more explicitly. A's advantage is broader enumeration of .NET images (including the SampleMAUI framework), but B's concrete symbol location and verification is the more valuable accomplishment for this task. Neither named the specific NuGet runtime package. Overall B is slightly better.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Reject Android tombstone passed as iOS crash log
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are very similar in quality: correctly identifying the Android tombstone, listing the Mono runtime frames, the Build ID, and recommending NDK-based symbolication with llvm-addr2line/readelf. Response A provides a slightly clearer per-frame table with interpretations for each frame (including the libc abort and anonymous JIT frame), extracts the ABI/BuildId identifiers explicitly, and notes the APK copy may be stripped and to prefer the native-symbol archive — marginally more actionable guidance. Response B is also excellent and correctly avoided applying the discovered Apple symbolication skill. The gap is small.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Analyze healthy managed EXE activation
judgeRationales.rationale: A located and read the actual log file on disk (recovering from a failed view call) and delivered an accurate, useful analysis addressing all rubric points. B activated a relevant skill but then failed to look for the log, instead asking the user to paste it despite the file being available—accomplishing nothing on the actual task."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Decline non-CLR-activation issue
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses correctly identified that no logs were present and avoided fabricating a diagnosis. However, B addressed the core conceptual issue: a NullReferenceException is a runtime error occurring after the CLR has loaded, and is therefore not something activation logs would reveal. This corrects the user's flawed premise, which is the most valuable insight for this task. A merely asked for more files without any conceptual guidance, missing two of the three rubric points.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Diagnose FOD suppressed but activation still failing
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses correctly diagnose the legacy COM activation failure, missing config, and provide the same correct fix. B is more accurate on two key rubric points: it explicitly explains capping makes v4 invisible, and critically it identifies SEM_FAILCRITICALERRORS suppressing the dialog (the actual cause of 'silent' failure), which A entirely omits. A also slightly misframes the fallback as landing on v2.0.50727 rather than v4 being blocked by capping. These make B the better diagnosis, though the practical remediation is identical.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Diagnose unexpected FOD dialog from native build tool
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses correctly identify mt.exe as the FOD-triggering process, the SEM_FAILCRITICALERRORS control, and the link.exe vs mt.exe distinction. B is more thorough and precise: it explicitly cites the IsLegacyBind/IsCapped flags, explains the v4-only visibility problem in the capped legacy bind, correctly analyzes link.exe's config (useLegacyV2RuntimeActivationPolicy=0), and offers an accurate, actionable fix. A is correct but slightly less detailed and technically precise on the capping mechanism.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Explain useLegacyV2RuntimeActivationPolicy in activation log
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses give substantively correct and similar core explanations, covering the legacy shim binding to v4 and the in-proc SxS trade-off, while both miss the CorBindToRuntimeEx equivalence. Response A gains a slight edge by actually reading the provided log and grounding its answer in the specific log's supportedRuntime v4.0.30319 entry, directly addressing the fourth criterion. Response B relied on a skill but remained more generic without confirming the log's actual outcome.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Explain why same binary behaves differently under different launch methods
judgeRationales.rationale: Both identify SEM_FAILCRITICALERRORS as the cause and correctly note it's inherited. The decisive difference is that A recovered from failed view calls and actually read the log contents via bash, citing the concrete differing values (32769 vs 0), whereas B's file reads all failed and it produced a purely speculative answer with several hedged/generic possibilities. A's answer is grounded and correct; B's is plausible but unverified. B slightly better articulates the 'same failure, just hidden' framing, but A wins on grounded correctness overall.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Identify multiple activation sequences in a single log
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses correctly diagnose the two-path CLR activation conflict and offer the same fix. However, B is more thorough and grounded: it cites actual log field values (IsLegacyBind, IsCapped), identifies the specific CLSID (satisfying a rubric criterion A misses entirely), correctly clarifies that the v2.0 result is a hypothetical FOD/NetFx3 suggestion rather than an actual v2 load, and notes SEM_FAILCRITICALERRORS suppressing the dialog. A is accurate but somewhat less precise and omits the CLSID. B wins slightly overall, largely due to the CLSID criterion and greater technical grounding.

verdictEvidence.reason: Net win +76.5% (15W/0T/2L over 17 stimulus vote(s), sign test p=0.001), mean preference +48.2% across 17 paired run(s) — credibly better

judgeRationales.scenarioName: .NET 10 on Linux with root access and native call stacks
judgeRationales.rationale: B correctly identifies and demonstrates dotnet-trace collect-linux, the ideal tool for .NET 10 on kernel 6.8 with root, matching the rubric precisely. A gives a reasonable but dated perf/perfcollect answer that misses the intended modern approach. B is clearly stronger on three of four criteria; the fallback criterion is a wash. Both are accurate and error-free, but B directly answers what the task rewards."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: .NET Framework on Windows without admin privileges
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are solid and accurate. B aligns more precisely with the rubric's emphasis: it centers PerfView as the primary .NET Framework tool requiring admin, explicitly notes dotnet-trace doesn't work with .NET Framework, and provides a concrete PerfView command. A is more comprehensive on process-level counters and dumps but treats PerfView as a minor item and never addresses dotnet-trace. Given the rubric focus, B edges ahead, though A's dump guidance is slightly richer.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Assembly loading failure on Linux (.NET 8)
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are strong, correct, and cover LoaderExceptions logging, COREHOST_TRACE, and the launch form. The key differentiator is the CLR event selection: B uses --clrevents assemblyloader, exactly the intended assembly-loader keyword matching the rubric. A uses 0x8:4, which is the Binder keyword rather than the AssemblyLoader keyword (0x4), making it slightly less precise. A adds strace as a nice extra, but B's core recommendation is more accurate for the stated goal. B is slightly better overall.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Container installation without .NET SDK
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses miss the aka.ms direct download links and curl/wget approach that the rubric emphasizes, instead using the SDK-image install pattern. Both correctly explain the SDK isn't needed in the target container. Response B additionally mentions kubectl cp, satisfying that criterion, and correctly adds the cpu-sampling profile relevant to the high-CPU scenario, plus analysis tools. Response A includes useful details on SYS_PTRACE and process namespace sharing. Overall B edges ahead by satisfying the kubectl cp criterion, though both are broadly comparable and both miss the primary intended solution.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Excessive GC on Linux (.NET 8)
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are largely equivalent and correct. B is slightly better because it explicitly addresses the collect-linux caveat for .NET 8, and adds useful handoff metadata guidance. A also offers a helpful raw-provider fallback, but B's explicit version-aware note aligns better with the rubric's fourth criterion.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: HTTP 500s from downstream service on Linux (.NET 8)
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are correct and satisfy the core rubric criteria: dotnet-trace with System.Net.Http, status codes for 5xx, timing correlation, a concrete command, and no collect-linux. B is slightly better because it includes additional relevant networking providers (DNS, TLS, sockets), the thread-time profile to see where slow calls wait, PID identification steps, and handoff details—all of which make it more complete and actionable for diagnosing intermittent slow/failing calls. A is more concise and adds a useful OpenTelemetry suggestion, but B's technical completeness gives it a slight edge."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Hang or deadlock diagnosis on Linux
judgeRationales.rationale: Response B aligns strongly with the intended diagnostic workflow: start with a trace to observe thread behavior (detecting livelock, starvation, or forward progress), then escalate to a dump only if a true deadlock is suspected, analyzed with dotnet-dump/SOS or LLDB/SOS. It hits all five rubric criteria. Response A is a solid, thorough answer but leads with dumps rather than a trace, omits livelock and lldb/SOS mentions, and doesn't frame the dump as a conditional follow-up. Both are technically competent and error-free, but B matches the rubric substantially better.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: High CPU in Kubernetes on Linux (.NET 8)
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are strong, accurate, and cover the core rubric points (dotnet-trace, dotnet-monitor, kubectl cp, avoiding collect-linux). B is better targeted: it clearly leads with dotnet-trace as the preferred approach, provides explicit install commands (dotnet tool install), and specifically frames dotnet-monitor for the no-shell case. A is more comprehensive overall (counters, dumps, throttling checks, security notes) which adds value, but it omits the specific install command and buries dotnet-trace behind counters. Given the rubric emphasis, B edges ahead, though A's broader guidance keeps the gap modest.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Kubernetes with console access prefers console tools
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses meet all three rubric criteria well and deliver correct, actionable guidance. A explicitly specifies the cpu-sampling profile, which is the direct answer to a CPU trace question, and mentions the diagnostics-disabled gotcha (DOTNET_EnableDiagnostics=0) which is a valuable practical detail. B is also excellent — it correctly navigated its skill references, avoided the .NET 10-only collect-linux tool, recommended perfcollect for native code, and includes helpful install/documentation steps. The differences are minor; A's explicit cpu-sampling profile gives it a very slight edge for the specific question asked, but overall they are near-equivalent in quality.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Linux pre-.NET 10 needing native call stacks
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are correct and cover the core rubric points well, recommending perfcollect, noting root requirement, and explaining dotnet-trace misses native frames. Response A is slightly stronger: it explicitly addresses why dotnet-trace collect-linux isn't appropriate for .NET 8, uses the current DOTNET_ env var prefix, and provides a practical fallback (perf record -g on the running PID) suited to the already-running app scenario.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Long-running intermittent issue with PerfView triggers
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are technically correct and well-structured, recommending PerfView with /StopOnPerfCounter and a circular buffer via Task Scheduler. B edges ahead by including both /BufferSizeMB and /CircularMB (matching the rubric explicitly), explicitly stating the trigger must fire on the spike start not recovery, and providing a practical Get-Counter command to find instance names. A adds useful extras (re-arm loop, disk space caveats) but misses /BufferSizeMB and doesn't make the 'fire on event not recovery' point as clearly. The gap is modest.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Memory leak on .NET Framework Windows
judgeRationales.rationale: Response B aligns much more closely with the rubric: it emphasizes two dumps for diffing, recommends a PerfView trace during growth, explains diffing to identify increased objects, and explicitly advises against waiting for OOM. Response A is broad and thorough on perfmon counters and general diagnostics, but misses PerfView tracing entirely and actually recommends capturing at the failure threshold/after OOM, contradicting a key rubric point. While A is more comprehensive on counters, B better matches the intended, focused methodology across nearly all criteria." [Magnitude reduced to "slightly-better": the position-swapped pass judged this "slightly-better", so the more confident "much-better" was downgraded.]

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Memory leak on Linux (.NET 8)
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are strong, methodical, and technically accurate. B better satisfies the rubric: it properly recommends dotnet-trace with gc-verbose during growth for allocation tracking (a key differentiator), uses skill-oriented phrasing for dump collection rather than hardcoding dotnet-dump, and activated the diagnostic skill. A is more comprehensive on native-memory and runtime counters, but misses the emphasis on allocation-tracing during growth. Both correctly avoid collect-linux and cover dump diffing. Net edge to B.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Networking timeouts on Windows with admin (.NET 8)
judgeRationales.rationale: B aligns closely with the rubric's intended answer (PerfView /ThreadTime with networking providers, correlating thread-blocking with networking events, RequestFailed events). It also used the skill to ground its answer. A gives a competent, methodical alternative (netsh trace, dotnet-trace, DNS/connectivity checks) but misses the specific PerfView thread-time approach and RequestFailed events the rubric rewards. Both share the networking providers criterion. Overall B is much better against this rubric.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Slow requests on Windows with PerfView
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are strong and correctly recommend PerfView /ThreadTime with good explanations and no default stop trigger. B is superior on the buffer-size criterion, including both /BufferSizeMB and /CircularMB (matching the rubric), whereas A omits /BufferSizeMB. B also grounds its answer in the loaded skill reference and adds relevant ASP.NET/Kestrel provider guidance. A offers a valuable caveat about async delays not appearing as blocked threads, but this doesn't outweigh the missing buffer argument. Overall B is slightly better.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Windows container high CPU with PerfView
judgeRationales.rationale: Response B correctly identifies that the user has host admin access and leverages PerfView from the Windows node with /EnableEventsInContainers, which is the accurate and preferred approach for process-isolated Windows containers. It hits all three rubric criteria including symbol merging and PerfViewCollect merge /ImageIDsOnly, plus adds useful artifact-recording guidance. Response A takes the wrong primary path (in-container dotnet-trace), explicitly downplaying the host access that the user specifically mentioned, and misses all rubric points about PerfView. Despite some tool errors in B's timeline, its final output is substantially more correct and complete.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Advisory: CoreCLR Alpine Docker non-root configuration
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are accurate and cover the key rubric points: env vars, SYS_PTRACE, dump directory permissions, no false Alpine workarounds, and advisory-only. B is slightly more complete and practical—it explicitly addresses host volume UID ownership (a real non-root pitfall), includes the full docker run command with volume mount, and notes musl/createdump compatibility plus version-specific naming token caveats. A is also solid and adds seccomp nuance, but B's guidance is marginally more actionable and organized.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Advisory: NativeAOT Kubernetes dump collection setup
judgeRationales.rationale: B satisfies all five rubric criteria, including the critical SYS_PTRACE capability that A omits entirely. B also correctly uses the full executable path for DOTNET_DbgCreateDumpToolPath, whereas A incorrectly claims the variable expects a directory. A does add some valuable caveats (SIGKILL/OOM not captured, symbol preservation), but the missing SYS_PTRACE and the incorrect tool-path guidance are significant correctness gaps. B is clearly better overall."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Advisory: macOS NativeAOT crash dump recovery steps
judgeRationales.rationale: Both give solid, correct answers covering /cores, DiagnosticReports, and LLDB save-core. B more sharply frames the already-crashed scenario, clearly distinguishing recoverable artifacts and emphasizing that ulimit must be set beforehand, plus notes .ips reports. A adds a reproduce-under-LLDB step and symbol preservation, which is useful but slightly off the 'already crashed' framing. B is slightly better on the core rubric points; A is cleaner operationally, but the task emphasizes output quality. Net: B slightly better.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Configure CoreCLR dump collection in Alpine Docker as non-root
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are well-formed and correct on most criteria, but B includes the critical --cap-add=SYS_PTRACE capability which is required for createdump to function in a container. A omits this entirely, which would cause dump collection to fail. B also correctly notes the .NET version dependency of the %e/%p/%t format specifiers. This makes B's answer functionally complete where A's would fail at runtime.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Configure automatic crash dumps for CoreCLR app on Linux
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: A, reverse: B). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Decline dump analysis request
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses miss the core intent: dump analysis is out of scope (the skill is dump-collection only), and neither states this. Both offer to analyze the dump instead of redirecting. However, Response B explicitly names out-of-scope tools (dotnet-dump analyze, LLDB) and, having discovered the dump-collect skill references, still ignored the scope boundary — making it slightly worse. Response A stays more generic. Both are weak, but A edges ahead slightly.

judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: B, reverse: A). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Recover crash dump from macOS NativeAOT without createdump
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses correctly cover the DiagnosticReports locations and avoid analyzing dumps. However, Response A additionally checks /cores for core files and mentions ulimit -c, directly addressing two rubric criteria that Response B misses. Response B's LLDB suggestion is only useful for a future run, not for finding an existing crash artifact. Response A is more complete against the rubric, making it slightly better overall."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Set up NativeAOT crash dumps with createdump in Kubernetes
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses correctly configure the tool path, volume mount, and dump type 4. The decisive difference is B includes the SYS_PTRACE capability (and seccomp), which is genuinely important for createdump to function in a locked-down Kubernetes environment—A omits this entirely. A does have a slightly more accurate note that type 4 is required for NativeAOT (B's comment misleadingly offers type 2), and adds fsGroup/sizeLimit niceties. But the missing SYS_PTRACE in A is a more consequential functional gap, making B slightly better overall.

judgeRationales.rationale: B is more exact about the eight executable ToLower sites and more concretely explains the compound allocation pattern. Both reach the key high-value fixes. B's unsealed-class recommendation is a weak, likely negligible optimization, while A's cache suggestion is speculative, so neither is flawless; B nevertheless has a modest edge in core analysis precision.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Detects Aggregate+Replace chain and struct missing IEquatable
judgeRationales.rationale: B satisfies every requested rubric item, provides a clearer structured scan, and distinguishes positive existing choices. A has useful additional hot-path observations (notably Log10/Pow and formatting allocations), so the overall advantage is modest rather than large.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Detects CurrentCulture comparer and compiled regex budget in inflection rules
judgeRationales.rationale: Both reviews find the key comparer and compiled-regex issues and offer useful fixes. B is modestly stronger through more precise counts, line references, and a correct single-pass Replace proposal, while A adds worthwhile CultureInvariant coverage but is less precise on the rule count.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Detects compiled regex startup budget and regex chain allocations
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: A, reverse: B). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Finds StringComparison.Ordinal missing and FrozenDictionary opportunities
judgeRationales.rationale: Both satisfy every required finding and correctly handle the mutable cache. B is somewhat more actionable through precise locations, comprehensive counts, the .NET 8 caveat, and a concrete recursive StringBuilder-helper direction. Its claims that concatenation is necessarily quadratic and that sealing is a notable hot-path win are somewhat overstated, so the advantage is only slight.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Finds branched Replace chain in format string manipulation
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: A, reverse: B). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Finds hot-path allocations in string humanization
judgeRationales.rationale: Both are strong and cover the principal requested hotspots, but A is more directly tied to the actual costly expressions and additionally flags the unconditional Humanize regex check, a consequential omission in B. B offers useful extra Split observations, but is more verbose, includes a dubious culture-correctness framing for user-facing title casing, and its sample rewrite is less polished.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Finds repeated enumeration in time and collection formatting
judgeRationales.rationale: Both reviews satisfy the core performance findings and preserve the fixture. A is modestly stronger because it explicitly catches the double projection overload, covers additional important formatting allocations, and prioritizes recommendations more clearly.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Flags Span inconsistencies and compound method chains in truncation library
judgeRationales.rationale: Both surface the principal allocation problems and give useful fixes. A is more disciplined about prioritization and applicability, avoids B's dubious unsealed-class recommendation and overconfident severity framing, and adds a relevant Unicode correctness caveat. B is somewhat more explicit about the Span inconsistency, but not enough to outweigh its less reliable extra claims.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Identifies unsealed leaf classes and locale hierarchy patterns
judgeRationales.rationale: Both apply essentially the same valid sealing changes and verify compilation, but B avoids A's overly broad claim that sealing necessarily resolves interface dispatch by clearly noting the limitation at interface-typed call sites. Both miss the requested positive observation about StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Decline non-CLR-activation issue
judgeRationales.rationale: B directly and accurately addresses the requested diagnostic category, explains its actual scope, and asks targeted follow-up questions. A reaches the same broad conclusion but materially mischaracterizes CLR activation logs and substitutes Fusion logs, undermining its technical reliability.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Diagnose FOD suppressed but activation still failing
judgeRationales.rationale: B gives a precise log-grounded diagnosis of COM activation, v2 capping, and the suppressed FOD dialog, while retaining the practical remediation. A has useful fixes but materially mischaracterizes the activation context and misses the core capping and SEM explanation.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Diagnose unexpected FOD dialog from native build tool
judgeRationales.rationale: Both reach the core diagnosis accurately, but B is more exact about the two activation paths and offers the materially better config remediation: useLegacyV2RuntimeActivationPolicy="true" is needed for legacy activation to bind v4. A's recommendation of false/bare supportedRuntime is misleading and may not resolve the underlying activation failure.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Explain useLegacyV2RuntimeActivationPolicy in activation log
judgeRationales.rationale: B captures the core semantics and critical SxS trade-off. A is substantially incorrect on both: it inverts what the flag does and states the opposite consequence for v2/v4 coexistence.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Explain why same binary behaves differently under different launch methods
judgeRationales.rationale: Both reach the core correct diagnosis, but A actually analyzes the available logs, cites their decisive exact lines and values, and gives a more direct, confident answer. B is somewhat more precise on the capped-bind terminology but unnecessarily asks the user to provide logs and includes less grounded ancillary advice.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Identify multiple activation sequences in a single log
judgeRationales.rationale: B supplies the central explanation for the reported intermittency: legacy activation ordering versus the independent modern CLR activation, plus the appropriate deterministic configuration fix. A gets many log facts right but incorrectly frames NetFx3/FoD installation as the standard/root fix and omits the key separate-bind/race mechanism.

verdictEvidence.reason: Net win +64.7% (13W/2T/2L over 17 stimulus vote(s), sign test p=0.004), mean preference +47.1% across 17 paired run(s) — credibly better

judgeRationales.scenarioName: .NET 10 on Linux with root access and native call stacks
judgeRationales.rationale: B directly answers the task with the .NET 10 Linux collection mode, its prerequisites, rationale, and usable command. A offers a plausible alternative diagnostic approach, but misses the preferred collect-linux workflow and includes questionable/confusing perfmap steps.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: .NET Framework on Windows without admin privileges
judgeRationales.rationale: B accurately communicates the central .NET Framework/non-admin constraint, avoids recommending dotnet-trace, gives dumps as a constrained fallback, and advises obtaining admin access. A is otherwise practical, but its claim that PerfView CLR EventPipe/managed CPU tracing works unprivileged for .NET Framework is a material error on the core question.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Assembly loading failure on Linux (.NET 8)
judgeRationales.rationale: B directly provides the correct, startup-safe assembly-loader collection workflow. A has useful supplemental advice (notably inspecting LoaderExceptions), but its primary provider-mask recommendation is unreliable for the specified trace and it includes invalid/questionable ALC diagnostic code, reducing its diagnostic usefulness.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Container installation without .NET SDK
judgeRationales.rationale: Both are strong, practical answers with correct direct-download, architecture/libc, collection, and copy-out guidance. B is slightly better because it directly supplies the requested Kubernetes copy-in command and includes an in-container download path; A's Kubernetes alternatives and IPC-socket caveat are also useful.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Excessive GC on Linux (.NET 8)
judgeRationales.rationale: B more precisely fulfills the requested GC diagnostic workflow by making `gc-verbose` the recommendation and supplying its exact collection command, while explicitly distinguishing trace data from a dump. A is generally useful but its primary `gc-collect` recommendation and missing explicit verbose command fall short of the stated target.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: HTTP 500s from downstream service on Linux (.NET 8)
judgeRationales.rationale: Both satisfy the core diagnostic request. A is more focused and its command is more directly usable for capturing HttpClient request/status/duration data; B adds unnecessary thread-time/root discussion and a potentially invalid or confusing profile combination.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Hang or deadlock diagnosis on Linux
judgeRationales.rationale: B more directly follows the requested diagnostic progression: trace first to characterize activity, then dump/debugger for possible deadlock, and explicitly names lldb+SOS. A is also practical and arguably more operationally detailed, but its ordering and framing do not satisfy the trace-first and trace-escalation emphasis as clearly.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: High CPU in Kubernetes on Linux (.NET 8)
judgeRationales.rationale: B is more focused on the requested CPU-trace collection workflow and offers a practical SDK-independent installation path, while correctly limiting its recommendation to .NET 8-compatible dotnet-trace usage. A is also strong and adds useful counters, dump, and Kubernetes operational caveats, but its installation route is less directly reliable in a production runtime image. Both miss the requested dotnet-monitor alternative for unavailable console access.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Kubernetes with console access prefers console tools
judgeRationales.rationale: Both are strong, practical answers. A is marginally better because it explicitly sets the CPU-sampling profile and adds a useful diagnostic-socket/user/TMPDIR container caveat. B has useful installation architecture notes, but its default-profile characterization is less precise and the explicit profile in A is preferable for this question.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Linux pre-.NET 10 needing native call stacks
judgeRationales.rationale: Both answers identify the right basic solution and satisfy the core requirements. B is more direct, explicitly handles the root and .NET-version constraints, and gives clearer collection steps. A adds useful perf and symbol-debugging context, but its mixed-tool framing and questionable duration syntax reduce its practical clarity.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Long-running intermittent issue with PerfView triggers
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: A, reverse: B). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Memory leak on .NET Framework Windows
judgeRationales.rationale: B more directly satisfies the requested .NET Framework collection workflow, particularly the PerfView trace during growth and explicit OOM-timing guidance. A is also strong and adds valuable perf-counter and WinDbg/SOS guidance, so the overall advantage is modest.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Memory leak on Linux (.NET 8)
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: A, reverse: B). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Networking timeouts on Windows with admin (.NET 8)
judgeRationales.rationale: B closely fulfills every requested diagnostic-data criterion with a targeted PerfView workflow, exact provider set, collection command, and relevant event interpretation. A offers generally useful alternatives, but misses the requested PerfView/ThreadTime approach and the explicit RequestFailed diagnostic detail; it also incorrectly calls 30 seconds HttpClient's default timeout.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Slow requests on Windows with PerfView
judgeRationales.rationale: Both identify the correct trace and explain it well, but B better matches the requested operational guidance by including explicit larger buffer and circular-buffer arguments and explicitly avoiding a default stop trigger.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Windows container high CPU with PerfView
judgeRationales.rationale: B satisfies all specified Windows-container host-tracing and analysis requirements, including the essential container ETW switch and symbol-handling workflow. A provides a plausible general dotnet-trace fallback but recommends the wrong primary approach for the scenario and omits every required PerfView detail.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Windows modern .NET with admin high CPU
judgeRationales.rationale: B fulfills all requested PerfView-focused requirements with a suitable collection command and actionable analysis steps. A gives a plausible alternative workflow but misses the rubric's required preferred tool and PerfView procedure.

verdictEvidence.reason: Net win +66.7% (7W/1T/1L over 9 stimulus vote(s), sign test p=0.035), mean preference +46.7% across 9 paired run(s) — credibly better

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Advisory: NativeAOT Kubernetes dump collection setup
judgeRationales.rationale: B directly addresses the key .NET 11 NativeAOT requirement of configuring the non-default createdump path and accurately constrains dump type to full. A has consequential inaccuracies about both points despite otherwise useful Kubernetes volume and capability guidance.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Advisory: macOS NativeAOT crash dump recovery steps
judgeRationales.rationale: A covers the key additional macOS recovery source—DiagnosticReports—while still explaining OS cores and pre-crash configuration. Both include unnecessary dump-analysis guidance and some caveats of uncertain precision, but B's omission of crash-report recovery is more consequential.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Configure CoreCLR dump collection in Alpine Docker as non-root
judgeRationales.rationale: Both give a usable automatic CoreCLR dump setup with the required environment variable, writable dump path, and SYS_PTRACE. B better handles bind-mount permissions and avoids the misleading Alpine-specific framing, while A additionally strays into dump analysis. B has minor arguably unnecessary or version-specific details, but is materially better aligned with the requested setup and rubric.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Configure automatic crash dumps for CoreCLR app on Linux
judgeRationales.rationale: Both deliver the three required CoreCLR variables and workable verification. B better respects the requested collection-focused scope and avoids irrelevant analysis tooling. A is otherwise strong, including a realistic crash test and correctly escaping % for its systemd example, while B's unescaped systemd template and unsupported assertion that the directory already exists are minor weaknesses.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Decline dump analysis request
judgeRationales.rationale: B directly identifies the skill-scope limitation and avoids taking analysis actions. A is oriented toward carrying out dump analysis and installation, contrary to the requested constraints.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Detect runtime and configure crash dumps for unknown .NET app on Linux
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: B, reverse: A). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Recover crash dump from macOS NativeAOT without createdump
judgeRationales.rationale: B more completely answers both halves of the request: it covers the macOS crash-report path as well as where a preconfigured core dump would be, and explains the crucial pre-crash `ulimit` condition. A is clear and useful for crash reports, but omits core-dump discovery and loss conditions. B's claim that a crash report is always generated is somewhat overbroad, preventing a larger margin.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Set up NativeAOT crash dumps with createdump in Kubernetes
judgeRationales.rationale: B provides a directly usable and materially correct NativeAOT .NET 11 Kubernetes configuration, including the essential createdump path and full-dump type. A omits the required tool-path setting, proposes an unsupported dump type, and leaves the central behavior unverified.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Detects compiled regex startup budget and regex chain allocations

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Finds StringComparison.Ordinal missing and FrozenDictionary opportunities

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Finds branched Replace chain in format string manipulation
judgeRationales.rationale: A actually inspects and reviews the implementation, identifying several hot-path costs and offering concrete structural and formatting improvements. B merely asks for code despite the code being available to the agent, so it fails to address the task.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Finds hot-path allocations in string humanization
judgeRationales.rationale: B covers every requested hotspot, adds the missing per-match lowercase allocation and positive span-helper assessment, and gives concrete recommendations. judgeRationales.scenarioName: Finds per-call Dictionary allocation not hoisted to static
judgeRationales.rationale: B is a substantially more useful, traceable performance review: it prioritizes findings, gives locations, concrete fixes, impact explanations, and positive observations. A tersely claims fixes were made without showing a patch or verification; its timeline also indicates the rewritten file was placed in /tmp rather than clearly applied to the target repository. [Magnitude reduced to "slightly-better": the position-swapped pass judged this "slightly-better", so the more confident "much-better" was downgraded.]

judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: A, reverse: B). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.rationale: Both fail every requested substantive review criterion. A is nevertheless a clearer, direct request for the missing code, whereas B promises to load references without doing so and adds unnecessary/confusing process language.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Handle .NET frames with no BuildId metadata
judgeRationales.rationale: Both reach the correct core conclusion and avoid fabricated symbolication. B is modestly more actionable and directly explains the Microsoft symbol-server limitation and runtime-pack recovery path; A's addr2line guidance with a matching unstripped binary is also sound.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Recognize NativeAOT tombstone with app binary and libSystem.Native.so
judgeRationales.rationale: The responses reach essentially the same correct practical conclusion and recovery steps. B is marginally cleaner and avoids A's unsupported JIT characterization of the anonymous frame. B's final claim that the null dereference originates in app code is also stronger than the evidence supports, so the advantage is modest.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Recognize tombstone with no .NET frames
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: B, reverse: A). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Reject iOS crash log as wrong format
judgeRationales.rationale: B successfully inspects and classifies the log, avoids using the inapplicable Android workflow, and provides correct iOS dSYM/atos guidance. A cannot access the file and offers only a request to resend it.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Symbolicate .NET frames in an Android tombstone
judgeRationales.rationale: B best satisfies the central request by delivering a credible, specific symbolicated runtime backtrace with source locations and crash interpretation. A usefully documents how to fetch and invoke symbols, but its purported resolved frames are inaccurate/placeholder rather than the actual symbolication result.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Symbolicate CoreCLR frames in an Android tombstone
judgeRationales.rationale: Both correctly conclude that no actual runtime symbolication is possible without matching symbols, but B gives the requested llvm-symbolizer form and substantively verifies the symbol-server/local-symbol failure. A's alternate addr2line command is useful but misses the requested form and includes an unsupported claim that llvm-symbolizer is unavailable.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Symbolicate multi-thread tombstone
judgeRationales.rationale: B performs real BuildId-matched symbolication and reports precise symbols and source locations for every Mono frame across all relevant threads. A's core symbolication is materially wrong and appears speculative despite offering a useful command/script.

verdictEvidence.reason: Net win +100.0% (3W/0T/0L over 3 stimulus vote(s), sign test p=0.125), mean preference +80.0% across 3 paired run(s) — underpowered (3 counted stimulus vote(s); a credible verdict needs at least 5, and this eval won every one of them) — add distinct, discriminating stimuli; repeated runs do not increase task breadth

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Investigate root cause of a .NET MAUI iOS crash
judgeRationales.rationale: B performs a substantive, well-supported crash analysis, explains the managed-exception startup failure and practical next steps. A merely reports that it cannot find the file, despite the log being available in B's run. B's only notable omission is the more specific SDK/NuGet dSYM location guidance.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Parse .NET frames and locate dSYMs from an iOS crash log
judgeRationales.rationale: B is more complete on the runtime image set and materially succeeds in retrieving runtime symbols from the Microsoft symbol server, with broader atos coverage. Its framework dSYM path labeling and omission of a package/UUID-verification discussion prevent a large win; A has a better framework-specific dSYM command and verification tip but is substantially incomplete on runtime components.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Reject Android tombstone passed as iOS crash log
judgeRationales.rationale: Neither response could parse a missing file, but B gives accurate, actionable Android/.NET-native symbolication guidance and clearly distinguishes it from Apple crash workflows. A merely asks for the file or its contents.

verdictEvidence.reason: Net win +14.3% (3W/2T/2L over 7 stimulus vote(s), sign test p=0.500), mean preference +22.9% across 7 paired run(s) — not credible (sign test p=0.500 > 0.05)

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Decline non-CLR-activation issue
judgeRationales.rationale: B directly addresses the central conceptual mismatch in the request and correctly scopes what CLR activation logs can establish. A is appropriately cautious about missing artifacts but omits that essential explanation and implies activation tracing may help diagnose the managed null reference.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Diagnose FOD suppressed but activation still failing
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: B, reverse: A). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Diagnose unexpected FOD dialog from native build tool
judgeRationales.rationale: A actually finds and analyzes the supplied log files, identifies the direct dialog trigger and relevant activation/configuration/error-mode evidence, and proposes actionable mitigations. B fails to inspect the available logs and merely asks the user to provide them.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Explain useLegacyV2RuntimeActivationPolicy in activation log
judgeRationales.rationale: B gives the central activation behavior and the pre-v4 SxS trade-off substantially correctly, though it overstates the exact config source of the log line and does not explicitly demonstrate the particular log's v4 decision. A's core explanation is backwards, presenting the switch as a v2-forcing policy rather than enabling legacy activation paths to associate with v4.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Explain why same binary behaves differently under different launch methods
judgeRationales.rationale: B precisely answers the log discrepancy, correctly explains inherited SEM_FAILCRITICALERRORS and dialog suppression, and identifies the shared capped legacy-bind failure. A is confidently focused on an unrelated SxS theory and proposes unsuitable fixes.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Identify multiple activation sequences in a single log
judgeRationales.rationale: Both fail to provide the requested analysis and merely ask for the absent log. A is marginally more useful because it explicitly says no log is visible and invites the user to paste relevant excerpts, whereas B only generically requests files.

verdictEvidence.reason: Net win +64.7% (13W/2T/2L over 17 stimulus vote(s), sign test p=0.004), mean preference +50.6% across 17 paired run(s) — credibly better

judgeRationales.scenarioName: .NET 10 on Linux with root access and native call stacks
judgeRationales.rationale: B aligns with the task's preferred .NET 10 Linux collection path and gives usable collect-linux commands plus the key perf_events/native/kernel rationale. Its missing fallback note is a minor omission relative to A, which does not recommend or document collect-linux at all.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: .NET Framework on Windows without admin privileges
judgeRationales.rationale: B aligns with the .NET Framework/no-admin limitations and offers an appropriately constrained dump-based fallback plus escalation path. A contains central misleading recommendations: dotnet-trace does not support .NET Framework, and its asserted non-admin PerfView/ETW CPU-trace workflow is not valid.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Assembly loading failure on Linux (.NET 8)
judgeRationales.rationale: Both identify the correct runtime loader tracing approach and startup-launch collection. A is more broadly actionable and its launch command is valid for a framework-dependent DLL; it also correctly emphasizes inspecting ReflectionTypeLoadException.LoaderExceptions and offers host/ALC-level diagnostics. B's more concise clrevents syntax is strong, but its displayed DLL launch command is materially flawed and it overstates what loader trace events alone reveal.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Container installation without .NET SDK
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: B, reverse: A). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Excessive GC on Linux (.NET 8)
judgeRationales.rationale: B directly satisfies the core request and the explicit expected command/profile for .NET 8 GC diagnosis. A offers some useful supplementary material, but omits gc-verbose and substitutes a less clear manual provider configuration plus potentially distracting dump guidance.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: HTTP 500s from downstream service on Linux (.NET 8)
judgeRationales.rationale: B is more precise and directly actionable for the stated diagnostic goal, especially by naming RequestStop/statusCode and providing a clean networking trace command. A is broadly useful but contains questionable provider naming and some overbroad claims about what the trace alone exposes.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Hang or deadlock diagnosis on Linux
judgeRationales.rationale: B follows the intended trace-first workflow, provides a sensible dump escalation, covers all requested failure modes, and includes Linux SOS debugging. A has useful dump commands but is dump-first and misses key requested distinctions and debugger guidance.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: High CPU in Kubernetes on Linux (.NET 8)
judgeRationales.rationale: Both give useful, actionable dotnet-trace collection and trace-copy steps. B better satisfies the requested contingency by explicitly naming dotnet-monitor for situations without pod console access; A adds useful counters and dump options but misses that explicit alternative.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Kubernetes with console access prefers console tools
judgeRationales.rationale: A is more reliable for the requested workflow: it explicitly requests CPU sampling and correctly explains that a .nettrace file must be converted before opening in Speedscope. B's claim that the raw .nettrace can be uploaded directly to Speedscope is misleading, though its primary collection command is otherwise sound.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Linux pre-.NET 10 needing native call stacks
judgeRationales.rationale: B directly recommends the appropriate Linux/.NET 8 native-stack workflow, clearly handles the root prerequisite, and gives actionable collection instructions. A contains a significant technical error by presenting dotnet-trace as capable of capturing native frames, which can send the user down the wrong path. [Magnitude reduced to "slightly-better": the position-swapped pass judged this "slightly-better", so the more confident "much-better" was downgraded.]

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Long-running intermittent issue with PerfView triggers
judgeRationales.rationale: Both are actionable and cover the requested collection setup. B is slightly better because it directly explains the most important trigger-timing behavior for a circular capture; A offsets this somewhat with useful process-targeting and scheduling guidance.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Memory leak on .NET Framework Windows
judgeRationales.rationale: Both provide sound core collection advice. B better matches the requested workflow through explicit in-growth capture, an explicit no-wait-for-OOM warning, and clearer PerfView diff/allocation guidance. A adds useful diagnostics and counters, so the overall gap is modest.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Memory leak on Linux (.NET 8)
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: B, reverse: A). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Networking timeouts on Windows with admin (.NET 8)
judgeRationales.rationale: B is a focused, actionable PerfView collection and analysis procedure that satisfies every stated criterion. A offers some potentially useful alternatives, but misses the requested PerfView/thread-time workflow and includes questionable or irrelevant environment-variable advice.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Slow requests on Windows with PerfView
judgeRationales.rationale: Both identify the essential ThreadTime trace and explain it well. B better matches the requested collection guidance by avoiding a default automatic stop trigger and keeping the command focused, whereas A adds a 60-second cap and questionable extra collection options.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Windows container high CPU with PerfView
judgeRationales.rationale: B directly addresses the Windows-container host-admin scenario with the recommended collection mechanism and correctly handles symbol preservation for later/off-host analysis. A offers a plausible generic dotnet-trace workflow but misses the requested scenario's key host-side PerfView approach and all required analysis details.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Windows modern .NET with admin high CPU
judgeRationales.rationale: B directly fulfills all requested Windows/admin PerfView collection and ETL analysis guidance. A contains useful dotnet-trace guidance and a PerfView alternative, but misses the task's preferred-tool requirement and is less coherent about the resulting PerfView artifact.

verdictEvidence.reason: Net win +77.8% (8W/0T/1L over 9 stimulus vote(s), sign test p=0.020), mean preference +64.4% across 9 paired run(s) — credibly better

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Advisory: CoreCLR Alpine Docker non-root configuration
judgeRationales.rationale: B is concise and accurately focused on CoreCLR createdump: capability, writable mounted destination, and environment variables. A includes misleading/unnecessary kernel core-pattern and core-ulimit guidance (relevant to kernel-generated dumps rather than CoreCLR automatic dumps) plus spurious Alpine-specific dependency advice, which could send the user toward host-level changes that are not needed.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Advisory: NativeAOT Kubernetes dump collection setup
judgeRationales.rationale: B fulfills all substantive requested pod-spec settings, including the .NET 11 tool-path variable, minidump enablement/type, SYS_PTRACE, and output volume. A replaces the intended NativeAOT createdump configuration with a materially flawed host-level core_pattern approach and incorrectly says the relevant environment variables do not work.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Advisory: macOS NativeAOT crash dump recovery steps
judgeRationales.rationale: B more directly answers recovery after an already-occurred crash, explicitly checks both available artifacts and correctly frames the prerequisite for a core dump. A includes useful context but is less retrospective and adds unnecessary/possibly nonportable gcore and analysis guidance.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Configure CoreCLR dump collection in Alpine Docker as non-root
judgeRationales.rationale: Both contain the essential automatic CoreCLR dump configuration, capability, and writable volume. B is more focused and supplies a valid run command, while A adds prohibited analysis guidance and its commented multiline docker command is broken as written. B's reliance on an existing app user is a minor assumption, so the gap is meaningful but not large.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Configure automatic crash dumps for CoreCLR app on Linux
judgeRationales.rationale: Both provide the essential configuration. A has substantially stronger process-level verification, but B satisfies the explicit constraint not to install or analyze dump tooling and avoids A's misleading suggestion that SIGABRT can be used without killing production.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Decline dump analysis request
judgeRationales.rationale: B follows the skill's scope restriction, declines analysis clearly, and offers concise external references without attempting setup or analysis. A provides otherwise plausible technical guidance, but materially violates the required scope and tool-install constraints.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Detect runtime and configure crash dumps for unknown .NET app on Linux
judgeRationales.rationale: A is overall more reliable and complete for runtime detection and automatic dump configuration, especially through direct process-map inspection and systemd guidance. B avoids dump-analysis instructions, but its weak strings-only detection and misleading /proc environment-injection suggestion reduce its quality.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Recover crash dump from macOS NativeAOT without createdump
judgeRationales.rationale: B covers both macOS crash reports and the crucial `/cores` core-dump path, explains the pre-crash ulimit requirement, and provides useful next-run setup. A correctly locates crash reports but misses the core-dump portion of the request.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Set up NativeAOT crash dumps with createdump in Kubernetes
judgeRationales.rationale: B directly provides the required .NET 11 NativeAOT createdump path setting, SYS_PTRACE, full-dump configuration, and writable dump volume. A has a correct volume and enables minidumps, but omits SYS_PTRACE, uses an incorrect tool-path variable, and adds misleading/unnecessary core-pattern and dump-type guidance.

verdictEvidence.reason: Net win +100.0% (1W/0T/0L over 1 stimulus vote(s), sign test p=0.500), mean preference +100.0% across 1 paired run(s) — underpowered (1 counted stimulus vote(s); a credible verdict needs at least 5, and this eval won every one of them) — add distinct, discriminating stimuli; repeated runs do not increase task breadth

activationScenarios.scenarioName: Investigate runtime upgrade performance impact

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Investigate runtime upgrade performance impact
judgeRationales.rationale: Both produced real runtime comparisons using properly resolved BenchmarkDotNet, but B's results and interpretation align far better with the requested upgrade assessment. A's headline 4–8x gains and favorable UniqueWordCount conclusion are materially misleading, particularly given its acknowledged noisy .NET 9 measurements.
